10445-american-big-game-in-its-haunts-th:
George Bird Grinnell edited this 1904 book of the Boone and Crockett Club, founded by Theodore Roosevelt to save American big game. Roosevelt himself writes on wilderness reserves, while other members treat zoology, hunting, and the making of game refuges. The book joins sport to conservation at an early date.

Bear hunting on Kodiak, white sheep of Kenai, giant moose, mountain sheep, and trophies from India fill the chapters. Preservation of wild animals and distribution of moose add science to adventure. Readers get a landmark of American conservation writing, by hunters who became protectors.
17612-handbook-to-the-severn-valley-rail:
J. Randall, fellow of the Geological Society and author of a book on the Severn Valley, wrote this handbook to the Severn Valley Railway, describing places along the line from Worcester to Shrewsbury. This transcription follows a facsimile of the original 1863 printing and design. The book opens with the legend of the Severn, the Wye, and the Rheidol, rivers the Welsh proudly personify.

Welsh folk, Randall notes, give hills and rivers characters matching their features, and the legend sets the tone for a line-side guide. Readers get a Victorian railway handbook, useful for the railway, the river valley, and the legends tied to both. It suits railway historians and walkers of the Severn country.
20346-bell-s-cathedrals-the-cathedral-ch:
Philip W. Sergeant wrote the Bell's Cathedrals volume on Winchester Cathedral. His aim was a work of real value to students of archaeology and history. Yet it must not be too technical for an ordinary visitor or tourist. That balance guides the whole Bell's series on English cathedrals.

Winchester was a capital of Saxon kings and holds a vast Norman nave. The book walks readers through its shrines, bishops, and carved stone. Sergeant mixes dates and building facts with tales of the see. Readers get a clear, learned guide to one great English church.
26568-seventh-annual-report-of-the-burea:
J. W. Powell, director of the Bureau of Ethnology, sent this seventh annual report to the Secretary of the Smithsonian Institution for 1885-86, printed at Washington in 1891. The director's report surveys field work, mound explorations, stone villages, and office work by a large staff, from Cyrus Thomas to James Mooney. It records a year of survey, digging, and cataloguing across the country.

Three accompanying papers form the bulk of the volume. Powell contributes Indian Linguistic Families of America North of Mexico, W. J. Hoffman writes on the Midēwiwin, or Grand Medicine Society, of the Ojibwa, and James Mooney gives the Sacred Formulas of the Cherokees. Together they preserve language maps, medicine rites, and Cherokee texts from the bureau's early years.
american-big-game-in-its-haunts-the-book: George Bird Grinnell edits the Boone and Crockett Club's book on American big game in its haunts, with chapters on bear hunting on Kodiak Island and the Alaska Peninsula. Club members write of tracking, stalking, and the habits of game animals in wild country. The volume blends sport with early conservation feeling, valuing the animals it hunts.
doe-osti-17014405-fy26-annual-report-nuc:
Fiscal year 2026 annual report LA-UR-26-28599, issued October 1, 2026, covers a multi lab project to remeasure key gamma ray data for safeguards work. Katherine Schreiber of Los Alamos leads a long author list from several labs. The data are emission chances for uranium, plutonium, and americium in the 50 to 208 keV range, used by ultra sharp microcalorimeter instruments at the IAEA laboratory.

Year two centered on a plutonium measuring campaign shared by Los Alamos, Pacific Northwest, and Idaho labs, plus joint evaluation work with Lawrence Berkeley. Uranium results from year one were being finalized. One americium line at 164.69 keV stayed in dispute between old and new data, and the team flags a fresh measurement as the way to settle it.
doe-osti-17030323-data-cards-for-standar:
Diana McSpadden, Olga Kuchar, Charlotte Neher, and colleagues across several labs propose a shared data card for Energy Department linked data projects in this July 2026 report. A data card is a standard summary sheet for one data set. Many groups had built their own metadata habits, and the split made data hard to combine, govern, and reuse.

The framework merges those habits into one card that stays open to local additions. It draws on older documentation ideas such as Datasheets for Datasets and on public data standards including DCAT. Sections explain the card structure, how rival templates were merged, and the design rules meant to keep records clear, machine readable, and accountable.
doe-osti-2588740-mc-formula-protocol-for:
Taichi Kuroki and Shaun Onorato of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory are the technical contacts for this CRADA final report, NREL/TP-5700-95350, dated September 2025. Rich Myhre shares credit. With Frontier Energy and industry partners, the team built the MC Formula fueling protocol for H35 high-flow hydrogen, the standard meant for medium and heavy duty vehicles, in support of SAE J2601-5.

Fast hydrogen fueling is a thermodynamics problem: fill too fast and the tank overheats. The MC Formula computes a safe fill from measured conditions. NREL upgraded its H2FillS filling simulation on a high-performance computer to generate the protocol's fueling tables, within boundary conditions set by an industry survey. The tables were then proven in hardware. They were installed on NREL's heavy duty dispenser and on ZBT's H35HF dispenser, and fueling experiments followed. Commercial medium and heavy duty vehicles were fueled with the certified tables.
doe-osti-3001931-understanding-mechanism:
Dongsheng Li of PNNL watches crystals being born in October 2025. Nucleation, the moment dissolved ions gather into a first crystal seed, decides a material's phase and shape. It happens too fast and small to see with ordinary tools. Liquid phase transmission electron microscopy films it directly, electrons imaging a liquid cell while chemistry runs inside. An electrochemical version adds electrodes, so an applied field can steer the process.

Control experiments without a field set the baseline: precipitate morphology and composition, and how acidity shifts them. With the field on, the team mapped the safe voltage range. They then traced how the field moves ions and changes crystal growth. The role of the liquid cell's confining surfaces gets its own analysis, since walls can seed or block nuclei. Understanding selective nucleation feeds battery materials, mineral scaling and crystal engineering, anywhere the first seed decides the product.
doe-osti-3009172-tracer-map-mapping-aero:
Final technical report for DOE award DE-SC0021400 covers the TRACER-MAP campaign over Houston. Baylor University's Rebecca Sheesley led it as principal investigator, with co-investigators at Baylor, Houston, Rice, and UC Riverside. The period ran from September 2020 to August 2025, with fieldwork in summer 2022.

From July 1 to September 3, 2022, instruments mapped aerosols, gases, and weather at five sites. Two were urban, two industrial including the main TRACER site at La Porte airport, and one a forest background site. The mobile laboratory payload caught sea breeze passages and varied emission mixes across the metro area. New particle formation appeared on both rainy and dry days despite sharply different air conditions.
doe-osti-3011603-towards-commercializati:
Crack tolerant solar cell metallisation moves toward commercial production in the final report for award DE-EE0009013 by Osazda Energy LLC of New Mexico. Sang Han served as principal investigator over a project period from May 2020 to March 2025. The company offers a metal matrix composite silver paste, screen printed as gridlines and busbars on solar cells. Cell cracks from handling and weather drive the problem addressed.

The team estimated crack induced degradation costs solar farm owners over 17 billion dollars in lost revenue across five years. Full size module testing and field characterisation checked the paste under standard flash conditions at 25 degrees C. Reliability protocols targeted under five percent degradation for the modules tested.
doe-osti-3015294-big-data-meets-geotherm: Finding geothermal reservoirs with seismology is the subject of CRADA final report LBNL-2001734, dated January 6, 2026. Berkeley Lab contact Melanie Sonsteng ran the lab side, with Zanskar Geothermal and Minerals. It records no publications or inventions. Zanskar images subsurface faults and hydrothermal flow using micro-earthquake and ambient noise methods. Cheap seismometer arrays make that practical now. The team cataloged long-duration tremor-like events. It built three-dimensional shear-wave velocity models from Rayleigh wave data. It also tested a coherency grid search for small events. Field tests are next.
doe-osti-3377514-data-cards-for-standard:
A cross-laboratory report, version 1.0 and dated July 2026, proposes one shared data card for datasets across Department of Energy programs. Diana McSpadden of Jefferson Lab heads a six-author team from Oak Ridge, Sandia, Idaho, and Berkeley. Each program built metadata habits as data work grew. The habits clash: a dataset described in one lab reads as foreign in the next. The card aims for one core form, open to local add-ons.

The design leans on frames. It draws from Datasheets for Datasets and data statements in the AI world. Public standards set the base: the ISO/IEC 11179 family, DCAT 3.0, and its United States profile. Work from Project Alexandria adds fields. Goals named in the title guide the build: datasets should be transparent, interoperable, and governed. Later versions will fold in fixes as programs adopt the card. The report is a framework, not a mandate.
handbook-to-the-severn-valley-railway-il:
J. Randall, a fellow of the Geological Society, wrote this handbook to the Severn Valley Railway in 1863, the year after the line opened. It describes the places along the line from Worcester to Shrewsbury, for the traveler in the train. The book opens with the Welsh legend of the three sister rivers. They are the Severn, the Wye, and the Rheidol. The Welsh personify them in a tale about their lengths and the lands they water.

Town by town, the handbook tells what to see from the carriage window: churches, castles, coal pits, and famous views. Randall mixes history, geology, and local tale in the chatty manner of the early railway guide. The Severn Valley line became one of England's best-loved rural railways. This small book is its first portrait, made when steam in the valley was still a novelty.
